title: 2025-06-18 Redwood demo: JSON toolchain walkthrough — Zenly Inc.
next_steps: Share JSON schema examples and Console walkthrough recording
Set up technical POC with 1-week benchmark on private deployment
action_items: Samir: share example prompts & schema files by 2025-06-20
Maya: send pricing and pilot contract template by 2025-06-20
Marcus/Priya: provide sample dataset and SSO docs by 2025-06-23
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Zenly through JSON mode and function/tool-calling flow in the Console and discussed how Optimize can recommend batching/quantization profiles for their latency-sensitive chat product. Customer cares about strict JSON validation, guardrails for tools that write to their DB, and enterprise security (SSO/KMS/SOC2). Agreed next steps: share schemas, pricing, and run a short private POC for throughput/latency benchmarks.

[00:01:30] Samir (Redwood): (typing) first example: we ask the model to return a product recommendation object with fields: id, name, confidence, actions[] where actions can be 'search' or 'create_ticket' and we include a tools block that lists allowed tool signatures
[00:01:50] [automatic caption: inaudible]
[00:01:57] Lena (Zenly): when you say tools block, is that the same as function calling in other APIs?
[00:02:03] Samir (Redwood): yes very similar, we map tool names to your webhook endpoints or internal adapters. the Console lets you register a tool with a JSON schema for its input and an optional vetting script

[00:02:40] Priya (Zenly): sandboxed JS in control plane, what's the compliance story? we need auditable logs and optionally HSM-backed keys
[00:02:48] Maya (Redwood): we log tool invocation events, inputs (if customer allows), outcomes, and link them to the request id. For Private we can integrate with your KMS/HSM and keep the control plane logs in your VPC; also SOC2 certs and dedicated contracts available
[00:03:10] Samir (Redwood): back to the demo, i'm enabling strict_schema: true and switching to 'validate-only' mode to show how we reject non-conforming outputs before they're returned to the app
[00:03:25] [00:03:25] Samir (Redwood): (typing) prompt: respond with JSON only, follow schema. run model: LLama-2-13B-quant (demo model), response attempt 1...
[00:03:40] [00:03:40] Speaker 4: hmm

[00:05:30] Samir (Redwood): yes we have a trace view that records request/response, KV cache hits, batch grouping, and tool call logs. you can replay in dev-mode against a sandboxed endpoint
[00:05:44] Marcus (Zenly): what's the latency overhead of schema validation and vetting scripts? can we keep under 200ms p99?
[00:05:52] Samir (Redwood): vetting scripts are tiny and run in a separate fast-path; for simple checks we add ~10-30ms, schema validation is native in the runtime and typically sub-10ms; model inference dominates. In Dedicated/private with pinned GPU and quantized models you can hit the latency SLOs you described
[00:06:10] [00:06:10] Lena (Zenly): talk about Optimize — how do we get batching suggestions without breaking latency for single-user flows
[00:06:18] Maya (Redwood): Optimize analyzes real traffic traces and suggests per-route batching profiles. For low-latency routes we recommend small max-batch sizes + dynamic preemption. We also recommend KV prefix caching for repeated context to reduce token costs
[00:06:35] Samir (Redwood): showing Optimize tab: here's a suggestion to quantize to int8 for the generate route and enable burst pools for peak hours; it also estimates cost savings and model-quality delta from an eval set you upload
[00:06:50] Marcus (Zenly): quality delta? do you run evals automatically or do we upload eval prompts?
[00:06:56] Samir (Redwood): you upload a small eval corpus or use our built-in eval harness. Redwood runs A/B with baseline vs quantized (or smaller model variant) and reports accuracy metrics and hallucination rates per prompt set
[00:07:07] [00:07:07] Marcus: ok good
[00:07:10] Lena (Zenly): what about function calling security — can a model trigger a destructive tool chain? how do we prevent it
[00:07:16] Samir (Redwood): multiple layers: tool registration requires explicit name mapping, vetting scripts can enforce constraints, route policies can require human-approval for destructive actions, and for private deployments you can put the tool adapters inside your network so Redwood control plane just signals a safe invocation token
[00:07:34] Priya (Zenly): for compliance we need immutable audit trails and per-token billing breakdown
[00:07:39] Maya (Redwood): Console shows token-level cost attribution and audit trails tied to request ids. For enterprise we can push logs to your SIEM and retain them per contract
[00:07:52] [00:07:52] Samir (Redwood): now i'll show a live success scenario: model calls search tool, returns results, model decides to call create_ticket. watch the schema enforcement for create_ticket payload
[00:08:05] Samir (Redwood): (typing) response -> validated -> vetting script checks user_id exists in allowed namespace -> pass -> tool invoked -> webhook returns 200 -> Console shows event in trace

[00:08:39] [00:08:39] Speaker 2: uh huh
